questions.prompt: What is the typical purpose of the 'system' role in a chat-style LLM API call?
questions.referenceAnswer:
Answer: It sets instructions and policy for the model, usually invisible to the end user, established once at the start of the conversation

The system role is where policy and behavioral instructions live — tone, constraints, persona — typically set once and not shown to the end user, distinct from what the user actually says.
keyPoints: The system role is where policy and behavioral instructions live — tone, constraints, persona — typically set once and not shown to the end user, distinct from what the user actually says.

questions.prompt: What does tool calling let an LLM do that plain text generation alone cannot?
questions.referenceAnswer:
Answer: Produce a structured request to call a specific described function with specific arguments, which application code can then actually execute to take a real action

Tool calling gives the model a way to output a structured, executable-looking request (which function, with what arguments) rather than only prose — that structured request is what application code uses to actually perform an action like a database query or API call.
keyPoints: Tool calling gives the model a way to output a structured, executable-looking request (which function, with what arguments) rather than only prose — that structured request is what application code uses to actually perform an action like a database query or API call.

questions.prompt: Why does tool calling require the same security mindset as giving an untrusted party API access?
questions.referenceAnswer:
Answer: Because a model with tool access can be manipulated (e.g. via prompt injection) into calling tools with unintended arguments, the same defensive thinking used for any adversarial-input-facing system applies

Since tool calling gives a model the ability to trigger real actions, and that model can be influenced by adversarial or unexpected input (prompt injection), it deserves the same security scrutiny you'd give any system exposed to untrusted input.
keyPoints: Since tool calling gives a model the ability to trigger real actions, and that model can be influenced by adversarial or unexpected input (prompt injection), it deserves the same security scrutiny you'd give any system exposed to untrusted input.

questions.prompt: What tradeoff does fixed-size chunking make compared to semantic chunking?
questions.referenceAnswer:
Answer: Fixed-size chunking is simple and predictable but can awkwardly cut a sentence or idea in half at a chunk boundary, unlike semantic chunking's boundary-aware but more complex approach

Fixed-size chunking trades semantic coherence for simplicity and predictability, splitting purely by token or character count regardless of where sentences or ideas actually end — semantic chunking instead respects natural boundaries at the cost of more complexity.
keyPoints: Fixed-size chunking trades semantic coherence for simplicity and predictability, splitting purely by token or character count regardless of where sentences or ideas actually end — semantic chunking instead respects natural boundaries at the cost of more complexity.

questions.prompt: Why is application-level state management described as a 'genuine engineering responsibility' in this lesson?
questions.referenceAnswer: Since the model has no built-in memory across calls, the lesson emphasizes that it's squarely the calling application's job to store and manage what conversation state gets included in each new request.
keyPoints: Since the model has no built-in memory across calls, the lesson emphasizes that it's squarely the calling application's job to store and manage what conversation state gets included in each new request.

choices.text: Because the model itself is stateless, so the application must handle storing and deciding what history to include on each call
Because the LLM API automatically manages all conversation state without any application involvement
Because state management is entirely optional and has no effect on functionality
Because only the model provider is responsible for conversation state, never the developer

questions.prompt: Why does the lesson recommend correctly tracking message ordering across multiple tool calls?
questions.referenceAnswer: The lesson's stated common mistake is losing track of message ordering, which can cause the model to misassociate a tool's result with the wrong originating tool-call request.
keyPoints: The lesson's stated common mistake is losing track of message ordering, which can cause the model to misassociate a tool's result with the wrong originating tool-call request.

choices.text: Because tool results need to be correctly associated with their originating tool-call request, or the model can misinterpret which result belongs to which call
Because message ordering has no effect on how the model interprets tool results
Because only the very last tool result in a conversation ever matters
Because message order is automatically managed and can never go wrong

questions.prompt: What is the core observation behind the term 'lost in the middle', as introduced in this lesson?
questions.referenceAnswer: The lesson defines the phenomenon as models handling content near the start and end of a long context more reliably than content positioned in the middle, even when technically within the context window.
keyPoints: The lesson defines the phenomenon as models handling content near the start and end of a long context more reliably than content positioned in the middle, even when technically within the context window.

choices.text: Models attend more reliably to information near the beginning and end of context than to content buried in the middle
Models attend equally well to every position in a long context
Models cannot process any information placed in the middle of a context at all
The term refers to a bug that only affects very short contexts

questions.prompt: Why is showing unvalidated partial structured data to the user or downstream systems risky?
questions.referenceAnswer: A partially-streamed structured payload can appear reasonable while still being incomplete, so treating it as trustworthy before the full response has been validated risks feeding invalid or misleading data into downstream logic.
keyPoints: A partially-streamed structured payload can appear reasonable while still being incomplete, so treating it as trustworthy before the full response has been validated risks feeding invalid or misleading data into downstream logic.

choices.text: Partial structured data is always guaranteed to be valid and complete
Partial JSON can look plausible on the surface while still being incomplete or ultimately invalid, so treating it as final before full validation risks acting on incorrect or malformed data
This is never actually a risk in any real streaming system
Downstream systems automatically detect and ignore any invalid partial data

questions.prompt: Why should a good evaluation set deliberately include hard cases and known failure modes, not just easy examples?
questions.referenceAnswer: An eval set that only contains easy cases can't surface real weaknesses — deliberately including edge cases and known problem areas (echoing the red-teaming mindset from the generative AI course) is what makes evaluation genuinely useful for catching real issues.
keyPoints: An eval set that only contains easy cases can't surface real weaknesses — deliberately including edge cases and known problem areas (echoing the red-teaming mindset from the generative AI course) is what makes evaluation genuinely useful for catching real issues.

choices.text: Easy examples are always sufficient to catch every possible issue
Including edge cases and previously discovered failure modes is what actually tests the system where it's likely to fail, rather than only confirming it handles cases it would already handle easily
Hard cases should never be included in an evaluation set
Failure modes discovered from real usage are irrelevant to evaluation

questions.referenceAnswer: Validate arguments against the tool schema. Enforce authorization independently of generated text. Return a bounded validation error and limit retries.

Enforce authorization independently of generated text.

questions.prompt: How would you test that the change fixed this incident rather than hiding it?
questions.referenceAnswer: Keep a reproducible failing case for this incident. Return a bounded validation error and limit retries. Compare the same workload before and after the change; record both the target metric and regressions.
keyPoints: Return a bounded validation error and limit retries.
Compare the same workload before and after the change.
Check regressions as well as the target metric.

questions.prompt: The fix works in a small test but fails at production scale. What next?
questions.referenceAnswer: Validate arguments against the tool schema. Measure representative workloads and separate resource, data and configuration differences. Stage a rollout with a rollback condition and rerun the original failure case.
keyPoints: Validate arguments against the tool schema.
Measure a representative workload.
Stage rollout and define rollback criteria.
